name: Arunachal
tagline: Monasteries, rice valleys and India's wettest forests
meta_description: Plan Arunachal Pradesh: Tawang via Sela, Ziro's Apatani valley, Mechuka, Namdapha and the Siang. Permits, real INR costs, routes, homestays and best months.
summary: Arunachal is India's far eastern Himalaya: Monpa Buddhist country around Tawang and Dirang in the west, Apatani rice valleys at Ziro, Adi villages along the Siang, and the rainforest of Namdapha in the east. Indians need an Inner Line Permit, foreigners a Protected Area Permit. October to April is the best window.
intro: Arunachal Pradesh is the largest of the northeastern states and the least crowded part of the Himalaya we plan trips in. The mountains rise from about 150 m on the Assam plains at Pasighat to above 4,000 m at Sela Pass, and the people change almost valley by valley. More than two dozen major tribes live here, each with its own language, festivals and farming calendar, so a week in Tawang and a week in Ziro feel like two separate countries.

The west, reached from Guwahati and Tezpur, is Monpa country: prayer flags, stone houses, butter tea and the great monastery at Tawang, founded in 1680–81. The road climbs through Bhalukpong, Bomdila and Dirang, then crosses Sela Pass or, since 2024, the Sela Tunnel below it. This circuit has the most hotels, the most shared Sumos and the most travellers, and it is where most first trips begin.

The centre and east run on a different rhythm. In Ziro the Apatani farm wet rice with fish in the same paddies, a system on UNESCO's tentative World Heritage list. Along the Siang, Adi villages brew apong and dance at Solung each September. Mechuka sits in a wide valley close to the high frontier, and Namdapha, near the Myanmar border, protects lowland rainforest where tigers, leopards, clouded leopards and snow leopards are all recorded.

Distances are long and roads are slow. Two hundred kilometres can take eight hours, landslides close roads in the monsoon, and mobile data thins out beyond district towns. Plan one circuit per trip rather than trying to see the whole state, build in a spare day, and carry your permit papers. In return you get monasteries without queues, villages where visitors are still guests, and some of the cheapest homestays in the Himalaya.

story.title: How the eastern Himalaya was settled and kept

chapters.heading: A monastery asked for by a Dalai Lama
chapters.text: In 1680–81 a monk called Merak Lama Lodre Gyatso founded a monastery on a ridge above the Tawang valley, at the wish of the 5th Dalai Lama. It grew into the largest Buddhist monastery in India, with a compound wall about 925 feet long and room for several hundred monks. Two years after its founding, in 1683, a boy named Tsangyang Gyatso was born at Urgelling, a small temple a short drive below the town. He became the 6th Dalai Lama, remembered across the Tibetan world for his love poems. The monastery library still holds handwritten volumes of the Kangyur with gold lettering, and the Monpa of nearby Mukto village once made the paper, Mon shugu, from the bark of a local shrub.

chapters.heading: Fish in the rice, pine on the hills
chapters.text: The Apatani of the Ziro valley chose a different path from most of their neighbours. Instead of shifting cultivation on the slopes, they built permanent terraced paddies on the valley floor, fed by channels from forested streams. Fish are raised in the flooded fields and finger millet grows on the bunds between plots, so one field gives grain, protein and a second crop. The forests above are managed as clan and village land for pine and bamboo. India submitted the Apatani Cultural Landscape to UNESCO's tentative World Heritage list in 2014. With no salt deposits nearby, the Apatani also made their own salt, tapyo, from the ash of burnt plants, and many households still keep the custom.

chapters.heading: Sun, Moon and the river from Tibet
chapters.text: The great river of southern Tibet, the Yarlung Tsangpo, enters India in Arunachal and becomes the Siang. Below Pasighat it meets the Dibang and Lohit to form the Brahmaputra. The Adi villages along its banks follow Donyi-Polo, a faith centred on the Sun and the Moon, and mark the end of sowing with Solung in early September, with the long ponung dance performed by women. Pasighat, on the Siang where it leaves the hills, was set up in 1911 and is counted as the oldest town in Arunachal. Every gathering, from a village council to a wedding, is likely to begin with apong, rice beer brewed at home and poured from bamboo or gourd vessels.

chapters.heading: Four cats, one ape and a wet forest
chapters.text: At the eastern edge of the state, Namdapha National Park climbs from about 200 m on the Noa Dihing river to 4,571 m on the Dapha Bum ridge. That range packs lowland rainforest, oak and rhododendron, and alpine meadow into one protected area of 1,985 sq km, declared a national park and tiger reserve in 1983. It is one of the few places recording all four of tiger, leopard, clouded leopard and snow leopard. It also shelters the hoolock gibbon, India's only ape, and a flying squirrel known from Namdapha alone. The Singpho people living on its fringe near Miao are among the communities credited with drinking tea from native Assam plants long before British tea gardens began.

highlights.title: Tawang Monastery at morning prayers
highlights.text: India's largest Buddhist monastery, founded in 1680–81, sits on a ridge at about 3,000 m above Tawang town. Arrive by 6 am to hear the monks chanting in the assembly hall, then walk the lanes of monks' quarters and visit the small museum of old manuscripts and masks.

highlights.title: Over Sela Pass, or under it
highlights.text: The road to Tawang crosses Sela Pass at about 4,170 m beside a high lake that freezes in winter. Since March 2024 the Sela Tunnel offers an all-weather route below the pass, but most travellers still drive over the top on a clear day for the lake and the prayer flags.

highlights.title: Ziro's fish-and-rice valley
highlights.text: The Apatani farm a flat valley at about 1,500 m in permanent paddies where fish grow among the rice. Walk the bunds between Hong, Hari and Bulla villages in April planting season or September harvest, and stay with an Apatani family to taste pike pila and home-brewed rice beer.

highlights.title: Mechuka at the end of the road
highlights.text: A wide valley around 1,900 m on the Siyom river, 187 km beyond Aalo by a slow mountain road. Memba Buddhist and Adi villages share the valley, the Samten Yongcha monastery looks down from a ridge, and homestays light wood stoves on cold nights.

highlights.title: Namdapha's rainforest by the Noa Dihing
highlights.text: Sleep at Deban beside the Noa Dihing river and walk into one of India's largest protected forests with a forest guide. Hoolock gibbons call in the mornings, hornbills cross the river, and longer treks run several days deeper into the park on forest trails.

highlights.title: Dirang's orchards, hot springs and yaks
highlights.text: Dirang is the gentle middle of the Tawang road at about 1,600 m, with kiwi and apple orchards, a riverside hot spring and an old stone dzong village. The national research centre on yak has its main campus here, and the Sangti valley lies a short drive away.

money_savers: Book shared Sumo seats a day ahead at the Tawang, Ziro or Aalo Sumo counters; a front seat costs a little more but is worth it on long hill days.
Apply for your Inner Line Permit online before you leave home; the tourist e-ILP is cheap and saves a half-day queue at a check gate.
Homestays in Ziro, Dirang and Mechuka usually include dinner and breakfast, which can halve your food spend compared with eating in town.
Share a reserved taxi for the Tawang day circuit to Sela and the lakes with other travellers from your guesthouse; the vehicle price is fixed, not per head.
Travel in March, April or November rather than late October and late May, when Tawang hotel rates and taxi demand peak with holiday crowds.
Carry enough cash from Guwahati, Tezpur, Itanagar or Dibrugarh; ATMs in Mechuka, Miao and smaller towns can run dry, and the detour to find one costs more than the fee.
getting_there: Most trips start in Assam. For the Tawang circuit, fly or take the train to Guwahati, or fly to Tezpur, then drive north through Bhalukpong, where the Inner Line check gate stands; Guwahati to Tawang is about 450–500 km and usually takes two days. For Ziro and central Arunachal, fly to Donyi Polo Airport at Hollongi near Itanagar or take a train to Naharlagun, then drive about 115 km to Ziro. For Pasighat, Mechuka, Roing and Namdapha, fly to Dibrugarh; Pasighat is reached over the Bogibeel bridge and Roing over the Dhola–Sadiya bridge. Small airports at Pasighat, Ziro and Tezu have run limited regional flights, and a state-supported helicopter service links Guwahati with Tawang; schedules change often, so check current status before you travel.
permits: Indian citizens from outside the state need an Inner Line Permit (ILP). As we understand it, the tourist e-ILP is applied for online on the Arunachal Pradesh government's e-ILP portal, costs a few hundred rupees depending on length of stay, and covers the districts you list, so name every district you will enter. Foreign nationals need a Protected Area Permit (PAP), usually arranged through a registered tour operator; rules on minimum group size and fees have changed in recent years. Some border points such as Bum La need extra local permission. Check current status before you travel.

months.weather: Tawang −4 to 8 °C, snow likely; Pasighat 11 to 24 °C, dry
months.summary: Deep winter in the west and the clearest skies of the year. Tawang is cold and often snowbound, Sela Pass may close for hours after fresh snow, and the Torgya masked dances take over Tawang Monastery for three days. The foothills and the east are dry and pleasant, which makes January a good month for Namdapha, Pasighat and the Mayudia snow drive from Roing. Pack serious layers for anything above 2,500 m.
months.tip: If the Sela road is closed by snow, the tunnel route usually keeps Tawang reachable; ask your driver the night before.

months.weather: Tawang −2 to 10 °C; Ziro 3 to 17 °C; Roing 11 to 23 °C
months.summary: Still winter in the high west, with Losar, the Tibetan New Year, celebrated in Tawang in some years in February. Snow can lie on Sela and at Mayudia above Roing, which draws weekend crowds from Assam. Namdapha remains in its best dry-season window, and Ziro is cold, quiet and brown before planting. Good month for travellers who prefer empty roads and do not mind frost.
months.tip: Losar dates follow the Tibetan lunar calendar; check them before you fix Tawang nights.

months.weather: Tawang 1 to 13 °C; Dirang 6 to 19 °C; Ziro 8 to 21 °C
months.summary: Spring begins. Rhododendrons start flowering on the Bomdila and Dirang slopes, snow lingers on Sela, and roads are generally open across the west. Ziro prepares its fields and hosts Myoko, the Apatani spring festival of friendship between villages, in some villages each year. Namdapha is still dry enough for longer treks. One of the best all-round months to visit.
months.tip: Book Tawang rooms early if your dates touch Holi, when Assam weekend traffic rises.

months.weather: Tawang 4 to 16 °C; Ziro 11 to 24 °C; Mechuka 6 to 19 °C
months.summary: Warm days, cold nights and long views before monsoon haze. Ziro's paddies are flooded and planted, the best month to watch the fish-and-rice system at work. Mechuka is green and accessible, Sela is usually clear of fresh snow, and the Tawang lakes start to thaw. Pre-monsoon showers begin in the east late in the month.
months.tip: Carry a light rain jacket from April onwards; afternoon showers are common in the central valleys.

months.weather: Tawang 8 to 19 °C; Dirang 13 to 26 °C; Pasighat 21 to 31 °C, humid
months.summary: Summer holiday traffic heads for Tawang, especially from Kolkata and Guwahati, and rooms fill up. The high lakes are open and green, and Sela is at its easiest. Lower areas are hot and humid with rising rain, and Namdapha begins to close to longer treks. Go to the west early in the month and book ahead.
months.tip: Leave Tawang for Sela and the lakes by 7 am; clouds usually build by noon.

months.weather: Tawang 11 to 20 °C, rain; Pasighat 24 to 32 °C, heavy rain
months.summary: The monsoon arrives. Landslides become frequent on the Bomdila–Tawang road, the Aalo–Mechuka road and the routes into Ziro, and rivers rise fast. Tawang itself is green and quieter, but journeys can stall for hours. We avoid planning first trips in June unless there is flexible time and a strong reason to go.
months.tip: If you travel now, add two buffer days and keep flight bookings changeable.

months.weather: Ziro 18 to 27 °C, wet; Pasighat 25 to 33 °C, very wet
months.summary: Peak monsoon. Road closures are routine across the state and Namdapha's forest roads are impassable. The one strong draw is Dree, the Apatani agricultural festival held on 5 July in Ziro, which welcomes respectful visitors. Otherwise we suggest saving Arunachal for autumn. Leeches, mist and green paddy terraces are the reward for those who go.
months.tip: Leech socks and quick-dry clothing make July walking in Ziro far more pleasant.

months.weather: Tawang 12 to 21 °C, rain; Ziro 18 to 27 °C, wet
months.summary: Still monsoon, with the same landslide risk as July. Independence Day weekends bring some regional traffic to Tawang. Paddies in Ziro are tall and green, and Mechuka is lush but the road from Aalo can be slow and broken. Only for travellers with spare days and good rain gear.
months.tip: Ask your homestay host about road conditions each morning; local WhatsApp groups are faster than news reports.

months.weather: Ziro 15 to 26 °C; Pasighat 23 to 32 °C; Tawang 10 to 20 °C
months.summary: The rain eases through the month. Late September brings the Ziro Festival of Music, four days of outdoor concerts among the paddies, and early September is Solung, the Adi harvest-season festival around Pasighat. Rooms and Sumo seats to Ziro sell out for the festival weeks. The west clears gradually, with the first crisp days towards the month's end.
months.tip: Festival travellers should reserve Ziro beds and transport by June at the latest.

months.weather: Tawang 5 to 17 °C, clear; Dirang 11 to 23 °C; Ziro 12 to 24 °C
months.summary: The best month for most of the state. Skies clear after the monsoon, the Himalayan peaks show from Bomdila and Sela, and Ziro's rice turns gold for harvest. Puja holidays bring heavy traffic to Tawang in the middle of the month, so book early or travel late October. Mechuka and Namdapha open up as roads dry.
months.tip: Avoid driving into Tawang on the first days of the Puja holidays, when the Sela road jams.

months.weather: Tawang 1 to 13 °C; Pasighat 15 to 28 °C; Namdapha dry
months.summary: Cold, clear and quieter than October. Tawang nights drop below freezing, the first snow can dust Sela, and the light is excellent for photography. Namdapha's dry season begins, the best time for the Deban treks, and the Siang valley is pleasant for walks and river views. A strong month for the east and for value in the west.
months.tip: Pack a down jacket for Tawang even if the days feel warm at noon.

months.weather: Tawang −2 to 10 °C; Roing 12 to 24 °C; Ziro 2 to 18 °C
months.summary: Winter settles in. The west is cold but clear, with snow possible on Sela and in the Tawang lakes, which freeze over. Year-end holidays bring a short burst of visitors to Tawang. In the east, Namdapha and the Roing–Mayudia road are at their best, and the first snowfall at Mayudia draws day trippers from Assam.
months.tip: Many smaller lodges in high villages close for winter; confirm bookings by phone a week ahead.

faqs.q: Do Indians need a permit to visit Arunachal Pradesh?
faqs.a: Yes. Indian citizens from outside the state need an Inner Line Permit. As we understand it, you can apply online for a tourist e-ILP on the Arunachal government portal, upload ID and a photo, pay a fee of a few hundred rupees, and carry a printout. List every district you plan to enter, such as Tawang, West Kameng or Shi Yomi. Check gates at Bhalukpong, Banderdewa and elsewhere inspect it. Check current status before you travel.

Yes, with a Protected Area Permit. As we understand it, foreign nationals apply through a registered tour operator, pay a per-person fee, and receive a permit valid for about 30 days for named areas. Rules on minimum group size have been relaxed in recent years for some circuits, but border points need separate permission. Citizens of a few countries face extra restrictions. Check current status before you travel and apply at least two weeks ahead.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Arunachal Pradesh?
faqs.a: October and November are the best months for most of the state: clear skies, dry roads and harvest colours in Ziro. March and April are next best, with spring flowers and planting season. December to February suits travellers who want snow at Sela and Tawang or the dry season in Namdapha. June to August is monsoon, with frequent landslides, and we avoid it for first trips.

faqs.q: How much does a trip to Arunachal cost?
faqs.a: A saver trip with shared Sumos and homestays costs about ₹2,500–4,000 per person a day. With a private SUV and good hotels, plan on ₹7,000–12,000 a day per person when two share. Our 6-night saver Tawang circuit starts around ₹18,500 per person, excluding travel to Guwahati. These are indicative 2026 figures; peak October and May dates cost more.

faqs.q: Is Arunachal safe for solo women travellers?
faqs.a: Arunachal is generally regarded as one of India's safer states for women travelling alone, and homestay hosts are used to solo guests. Usual precautions still apply: reach your stay before dark, share your Sumo booking details with someone, and avoid isolated drives at night. Mobile coverage gaps are the bigger practical issue, so tell your host your plans for the next day.

faqs.q: Will I get altitude sickness on the Tawang trip?
faqs.a: Tawang town is about 2,670 m and the monastery about 3,000 m, while Sela Pass is around 4,170 m. Most people feel only mild breathlessness, but some get headaches at Sela or above Tawang. Sleep a night at Dirang or Bomdila before Tawang, drink water, and avoid alcohol on the first night. If you have heart or lung conditions, talk to your doctor before you go.

faqs.q: Is there mobile network and ATM access in Arunachal?
faqs.a: Jio, Airtel and BSNL have 4G in district towns like Tawang, Bomdila, Dirang, Ziro and Pasighat. Coverage drops on long road stretches and is weak or absent in Namdapha beyond Miao and in parts of Mechuka. ATMs exist in district towns but can run out of cash on holidays. Carry enough cash for homestays and Sumos, since UPI does not always work without data.

faqs.q: How many days do I need for Arunachal?
faqs.a: For the Tawang circuit from Guwahati, plan 6–8 nights: two days each way on the road and three nights in Tawang. Ziro needs 4–5 nights from Itanagar or Naharlagun. Mechuka needs 6–7 nights from Dibrugarh because of the long drive. Combining two circuits takes 12 or more nights, since there is no fast road between the west and the centre.

faqs.q: Can I take my own car or bike into Arunachal?
faqs.a: Yes, private vehicles from other states can enter with valid papers and every rider or passenger holding a valid Inner Line Permit. Mountain roads are slow, fuel stations are spaced far apart beyond Bomdila and Aalo, and monsoon landslides can stop traffic for hours. Many riders do the Tawang loop between October and April. Carry spares, and check current status of roads and permits before you travel.
